name: Hair tonic

lead: Hair tonic is a broad term for liquid preparations applied to hair and scalp. Historic tonics were scented grooming products, and modern versions range from sebum-control and anti-dandruff formulas to herbal tonics marketed for hair growth.
The appearance payoff depends on the formula: a cleaner, less greasy or flake-free scalp, easier styling, or in growth-oriented tonics the hope of denser hair.

paras: Tonics are applied to the scalp, usually after washing and often massaged in. Examples tested in trials include green tea, lemongrass oil, amla and teak leaf extract.
Plant extracts and essential oils can cause irritation in some people. Trials of the formulas above reported none with green tea tonic and described them as safe, though these were small studies.

chain: Liquid tonic applied to the scalp
Active (e.g. green tea, lemongrass) reduces oil or flakes, or is claimed to support growth
angle.text: Tonics are used to manage scalp oiliness or dandruff and, in herbal formulas, to try for denser hair. The effect depends on the specific formula.

lead: Hair tonic is a general name for liquid preparations applied to the hair and scalp. Historically the term covered scented grooming dressings that made hair glossy and easy to style; today it spans sebum-control and anti-dandruff liquids and herbal formulas sold for fuller-looking hair. People use them to keep the scalp clean and less greasy, to reduce flaking, to groom and style, and, with growth-oriented tonics, in the hope of denser hair.[1][2][3]

The best-known historical example is Macassar oil, sold by the London barber Alexander Rowland from about 1793 and used by Western European men through the nineteenth century and into the early twentieth.[4] A 1913 Texas Medical Journal editorial discusses the hair-tonic bottle as a fixture of the era.[1]

Modern research tests individual tonic formulations for specific cosmetic goals. A 2016 trial of a 2 percent green tea tonic in 20 volunteers found lower scalp sebum over 28 days, and a lemongrass-oil tonic was assessed for dandruff in a randomized split-head study of 30 people.[3][5] Herbal tonics for hair loss have also been tested, including a randomized trial of oral amla in women with androgenetic alopecia and a placebo-controlled trial of a teak leaf extract formulation in men.[6][7]
infobox: Green tea, lemongrass, amla, teak leaf tonics
Less oily scalp, fewer flakes, styling, fuller-looking hair

paras: Hair tonic has no single formula. Wikipedia redirects the term to its hair conditioner article, and the products grouped under it differ in base (water, alcohol, glycol or oil), fragrance and active ingredient.[2] Grooming tonics are mainly scented dressings; cleansing tonics aim at scalp oil or yeast-associated dandruff; and herbal growth tonics carry plant extracts such as green tea, amla, teak leaf or Cuscuta-derived oils.[3][5][7][8]

In traditional systems the phrase is also applied to plants. Reviews of amla (Indian gooseberry) list its use in Indian medicine as a hair tonic alongside many other traditional uses, and a 2024 trial states that amla has been described as a hair tonic in Traditional Persian Medicine, recommended orally and topically.[9][10][6]

subs.h: Macassar oil and the grooming era
paras: Macassar oil was a scented hair oil popularised by Alexander Rowland (1747-1823), a London barber who began selling Rowland's Macassar Oil around 1793. It was heavily advertised and became one of the earliest nationally advertised consumer products.[4] The original base was oil from the tree Schleichera oleosa, known in Indonesia as kayu hitam; as the tree was overharvested, makers moved to coconut, palm or similar vegetable oils scented with ylang-ylang.[4] A. Rowland and Sons registered Macassar Oil as a trademark in 1888.[4]

The oil's popularity left a mark on domestic life: because it rubbed off on chair backs, protective cloths called antimacassars came into use around the middle of the nineteenth century.[4][2] Lord Byron and Lewis Carroll both refer to it in verse, and an illustration by Thomas Rowlandson from about 1814 satirised advertising claims that the oil could regrow hair on balding men.[4] Later grooming products such as brilliantine and pomade followed the same dressing tradition.[4][2]

A 1913 Texas Medical Journal editorial titled The Hair-Tonic Bottle shows tonics were a familiar commercial category by the early twentieth century.[1] A 1973 German-language article in Medizinische Klinik discussed a Finnish hair tonic, indicating continued medical interest.[11] Recent scientific work has shifted toward standardised plant-extract formulations tested in controlled trials.[3][5][6][7]

A Thai study developed a tonic base of glycerin and butylene glycol (4 percent combined), which volunteers preferred, and incorporated green tea extract with the aim of reducing scalp greasiness; all products in the study were stable and none caused skin irritation in closed-patch testing.[3]

A tonic containing lemongrass (Cymbopogon flexuosus) essential oil, chosen for activity against lipophilic yeasts, was formulated and compared with a placebo base in 30 Thai volunteers with moderate dandruff on a D-Squame scale.[5]

Teak (Tectona grandis) leaf extract has been reported to inhibit steroid 5-alpha reductase, the enzyme that converts testosterone to dihydrotestosterone, which is implicated in male pattern hair loss; this was the rationale for a randomized placebo-controlled trial of a teak-based formulation in men.[7] Laboratory work on Lagerstroemia indica extract reported increased proliferation of human hair-follicle dermal papilla cells and reduced follicle degeneration in organ culture, alongside a volunteer trial.[12] A study of the Chinese Caizhixuan hair tonic examined apoptosis and PI3K/Akt signalling in androgenetic alopecia models.[13] Herbal oils made from Cuscuta reflexa stems in a mustard-oil base were studied for dandruff, hair fall and growth, with hair-growth effects tested in rats.[8]

In appearance communities, tonics sit alongside shampoos, oils and scalp serums as part of grooming and hair-density routines: a less oily scalp and a flake-free finish affect how hair looks and sits, while growth-oriented tonics are discussed as additions to other hair-loss approaches. Tonic bottles are mentioned only in passing in the forum threads on record, and no tonic-specific protocol has become established there.

Plant extracts and essential oils can irritate skin in some people. The green tea tonic study reported no irritation in closed-patch testing and the lemongrass and teak studies described their formulas as safe, though the trials were small.[3][5][7] Historically, hair tonics containing alcohol and other solvents have been swallowed by children; forum users recount stomach-pump hospital visits after drinking a bottle of a green hair tonic in childhood, a reminder that these liquids are for external use.[14]

A clinical evaluation of a 2 percent green tea hair tonic in 20 volunteers found significantly lower scalp sebum at days 21 and 28 (p up to 0.024) without irritation.[3] A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled split-head study of a lemongrass oil hair tonic assessed dandruff in 30 volunteers.[5] A triple-blind trial in 60 women gave oral amla syrup three times daily for 12 weeks; 52 completed, and the anagen-to-telogen ratio rose significantly versus placebo (p = 0.002), with higher physician and patient satisfaction.[6] A randomized placebo-controlled study evaluated a teak leaf extract formulation in men with androgenic alopecia.[7] The Cuscuta oil work combined human volunteers with hair fall and dandruff and rat growth experiments.[8] All of these tested specific formulas rather than hair tonic as a category.

lore.intro: Hair tonic is mentioned in training and appearance forums mostly in passing, and herbal growth claims circulate through traditional-medicine and product marketing rather than a defined community protocol.
